body:
The Political Importance of Lucknow

The Lucknow session of the Indian National Congress in December 1916 marked an important development in the national movement.

It is remembered for 2 related but distinct achievements:

  • The visible reunion of the Moderate and Extremist groups within the Indian National Congress.
  • An agreement between the Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League on a common scheme of constitutional reforms.

The second development is known as the Lucknow Pact of 1916.

Reunion of the Moderates and Extremists

The Congress had been divided since the Surat session of 1907.

Although organisational changes at the Bombay Congress session of 1915 permitted the Extremists to return, the reunion became especially visible at the Lucknow session of 1916, when Tilak and other nationalist leaders participated alongside Moderate leaders.

The President of the 1916 Lucknow Congress session was Ambica Charan Majumdar, also commonly written as Ambika Charan Mazumdar.

The reunion was important because nationalists who had disagreed over political methods could again operate through the same major national political organisation.

The Congress and the Muslim League

Background of the Muslim League

The All India Muslim League had been established at Dacca in 1906.

Its early concerns included protecting Muslim political interests and obtaining representation in government institutions.

Under the Indian Councils Act of 1909, commonly associated with the Morley–Minto Reforms, the British government introduced separate electorates for Muslims in legislative council elections.

This arrangement meant that Muslim representatives for the designated Muslim seats were elected by Muslim voters.

By the period leading to 1916, important Congress and Muslim League leaders increasingly recognised the advantages of cooperating in demanding constitutional reform.

The Lucknow Agreement

In December 1916, the Congress and the Muslim League held their sessions at Lucknow and adopted a common constitutional reform scheme.

Muhammad Ali Jinnah played an important role in efforts to secure Congress–League cooperation. Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Annie Besant also supported the agreement.

The two organisations agreed to press common demands for greater Indian participation in legislative and executive institutions.

A central part of the compromise was that the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims as part of the agreed constitutional scheme.

This acceptance helped the two organisations reach a common position, although separate electorates remained a controversial form of political representation.

Why the Agreement Mattered

Before the pact, the Congress and the Muslim League did not have a single agreed scheme for constitutional reforms.

The Lucknow Pact enabled them to present common demands to the British government while recognising particular Muslim representation claims.

The agreement became an important example of Congress–League political cooperation during the national movement.

It also demonstrated that the renewed nationalist mobilisation of the Home Rule period could support cooperation between different political organisations.

Distinguish the 2 forms of unity

  • Moderate–Extremist reunion: Unity between factions within the Congress.
  • Lucknow Pact: Cooperation between the Congress and the separate All India Muslim League.

The 2 developments occurred in the same political period, but they were not the same agreement.

Prelims focus

  • 1906: The All India Muslim League was established at Dacca.
  • 1909: Separate electorates for Muslims were introduced under the Indian Councils Act.
  • 1915: The Bombay Congress session permitted the return of Extremist nationalists.
  • 1916: The Congress session at Lucknow was presided over by Ambica Charan Majumdar.
  • 1916: Congress and the Muslim League adopted the Lucknow Pact.
  • Trap: The Congress reunion and the Congress–League Pact were 2 different political developments.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, 2020–21 edition, printed p. 114 and p. 124; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entries for the 1915 Bombay and 1916 Lucknow sessions, accessed 21 November 2026; All India Muslim League, Congress–League Scheme of Reform, 1916, resolution adopted at Lucknow on 31 December 1916, reproduced in All India Muslim League documents, Appendix 4, printed pp. 242–246; Bipan Chandra and others, India's Struggle for Independence, Chapter 13, The Home Rule Movement and Its Fallout, online text consulted 21 November 2026.]

title: The Lucknow Session of 1916: Congress Reunion and Congress–League Agreement

body:
What Did the Lucknow Pact Propose?

The Lucknow Pact was a joint scheme of constitutional reforms accepted by the Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League in December 1916.

It proposed greater Indian participation in government and arrangements for Muslim representation in legislative councils.

The pact was a political agreement presenting demands to the British government. It was not itself an Act of the British Parliament and did not automatically introduce all the proposed constitutional changes.

Demand for More Representative Legislative Councils

The agreement called for legislative councils containing substantially larger elected majorities.

It proposed that four-fifths of the members of the central and provincial legislative councils should be elected, while the remaining one-fifth would be nominated.

It also supported a broader electoral franchise and greater authority for legislative councils over administration and public finances.

The object was to reduce the dominance of nominated officials and increase the influence of representatives elected from India.

Indian Participation in the Executive

The pact sought greater Indian representation in executive government.

It proposed that at least half the members of provincial executive councils should be Indians elected by the elected members of the provincial legislative councils.

At the central level, it proposed that half the members of the Governor-General's Executive Council should be Indians, chosen by the elected members of the Imperial Legislative Council.

These were demands for reform of colonial institutions, not provisions already implemented by the pact.

Acceptance of Separate Electorates

The best-known feature of the Lucknow Pact was the Congress's acceptance of separate electorates for Muslims under the proposed representative system.

Separate Electorate

A separate electorate is an electoral arrangement in which voters belonging to a specified community elect representatives for seats allotted to that community.

In the arrangements discussed here, Muslim voters would elect representatives for the designated Muslim seats.

This must be distinguished from a joint electorate, in which eligible voters vote in a common electoral constituency rather than through separate community-based electoral rolls for designated seats.

Separate electorates had already been introduced under the Indian Councils Act of 1909. The important development at Lucknow in 1916 was that the Congress accepted their continuation in the agreed Congress–League constitutional scheme.

Proposed Muslim Representation at the Centre

The pact proposed that one-third of the elected Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council should be Muslims elected through separate Muslim electorates.

The qualification is important: the original scheme referred to one-third of the Indian elected members, not an unconditional one-third of every category of council membership.

Proposed Representation in Provincial Councils

The pact also specified different proportions of seats for Muslim representatives in the provincial legislative councils.

These proportions were not identical in every province.

ProvinceProposed Muslim share of elected Indian members
Punjab50%
Bengal40%
BombayOne-third
United Provinces30%
Bihar25%
Central Provinces15%
Madras15%

These figures belonged to the proposed Congress–League scheme of 1916. They should not be treated as present-day representation figures or as the composition of legislatures actually established in 1916.

The scheme granted Muslim representation above the community's population proportion in some minority provinces, while allocating a lower proportion in Muslim-majority provinces such as Punjab and Bengal.

The arrangements reflected an attempt by the Congress and the League to reach a mutually acceptable political compromise over representation.

Safeguard for Community Interests

The pact contained another important provision concerning proposed legislation affecting a particular community.

Under the agreed scheme, a non-official bill, clause or resolution affecting a community was not to be proceeded with if three-fourths of that community's members in the relevant legislative council opposed it.

The members of the community in that council would determine whether the proposal affected their community.

This was a proposed safeguard intended to prevent a legislative majority from proceeding with certain measures despite strong opposition from representatives of the community concerned.

Do not confuse the 3 numerical provisions

  • Four-fifths: Proposed elected share of central and provincial legislative councils.
  • One-third: Proposed Muslim share of the elected Indian members of the Imperial Legislative Council.
  • Three-fourths: Opposition by this proportion of a community's council representatives could prevent a specified non-official measure affecting that community from being proceeded with.

Constitutional Importance

The Lucknow Pact combined demands for representative government with specific safeguards for Muslim political representation.

It strengthened Congress–League cooperation because both organisations could press a common reform scheme before the British government.

At the same time, accepting separate electorates meant retaining community-based political representation. This became a lasting subject of disagreement in subsequent constitutional debates.

Prelims focus

  • The Lucknow Pact was agreed between the Indian National Congress and the All India Muslim League in 1916.
  • The Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims in the common reform scheme.
  • The pact proposed four-fifths elected membership in legislative councils.
  • It proposed one-third Muslim representation among elected Indian members at the centre.
  • The proposed community safeguard used a three-fourths opposition threshold for specified measures.
  • Trap: The Lucknow Pact did not introduce separate electorates for the first time; they had been introduced in 1909.

[Sources: All India Muslim League, Congress–League Scheme of Reform, 1916, resolution adopted at the League's Lucknow session on 31 December 1916, reproduced in All India Muslim League documents, Appendix 4, printed pp. 242–246, National Institute of Historical and Cultural Research PDF consulted 21 November 2026; Indian National Congress, Synopsis of Plenary Sessions from 1885 to 2018, entry for the 31st session at Lucknow in 1916, accessed 21 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, Chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, 2020–21 edition, printed p. 114.]
